name: Retinyl esters

lead: Retinyl esters are the form in which the body stores vitamin A, and cosmetics use retinyl palmitate, acetate and propionate as milder, more stable alternatives to retinol and tretinoin. The payoff people want is smoother texture and fewer fine lines with less irritation.
In skin they are described as converting to retinol and then retinoic acid, though absorption and conversion are said to be inefficient. No trials in the sources reviewed tested them for appearance.

paras: They are applied as creams and serums, often by people who find retinol irritating. Retinoid-type changes in skin generally build over months of regular use.
Excess preformed vitamin A causes hypervitaminosis A. Retinyl palmitate in sunscreens prompted a debate arising from a mouse study.

chain: Convert to retinol then retinoic acid
angle.text: Retinyl esters such as palmitate, acetate and propionate are milder, more stable forms of vitamin A used in creams. In skin they convert to retinol and then retinoic acid, aiming for renewal, smoother texture and fewer fine lines.

lead: Retinyl esters are fatty-acid esters of retinol (vitamin A) and the main form in which the body stores vitamin A, chiefly as retinyl palmitate in the liver.[1][2] In skincare, retinyl palmitate, acetate and propionate are used as milder, more stable alternatives to retinol and prescription tretinoin, with the aim of softening the look of fine lines, uneven tone and rough texture.[3][4]

The idea behind them is a conversion chain: in skin an ester is described as being hydrolysed to retinol, oxidised to retinaldehyde and then to retinoic acid, the form that acts on retinoid receptors in skin cells.[3][4] Reviews of cosmetic retinoids place esters in the first generation alongside retinol and retinaldehyde, and describe them as the gentlest and least irritating rung of the ladder.[5][4]

Published assessments differ on how much they do. A 2025 review concluded that retinol, retinyl esters and retinaldehyde used in cosmeceuticals are efficacious, safe and well tolerated, while an older 2006 review described retinol and retinyl esters as non-irritant but with only modest clinical efficiency.[5][4] Wikipedia notes that neither skin absorption nor conversion is very efficient.[3] Their use in sunscreens has also been the subject of a public safety debate.[3]

Retinyl esters sit at the gentle end of a wider retinoid family that includes retinol, retinaldehyde, prescription tretinoin and newer synthetic retinoids.[6][7] Because they are chemically more stable than retinol, which Wikipedia describes as unstable to light, oxygen, heat and heavy metals, they are a common choice in formulations where shelf life matters.[7]

paras: Cosmetic retinoids fall into generations. The first generation, comprising all-trans retinoic acid, retinol, retinaldehyde and retinyl esters, is the group mainly used for photoaged skin, with differing efficacy, tolerance and stability.[5] Tretinoin is regarded as the reference treatment but is prescription-only in most places, so retinol and its derivatives are built into over-the-counter products.[5]

Photoaging shows as wrinkles, laxity, uneven pigmentation and roughness, underpinned by epidermal thinning and loss of collagen and other matrix components.[5] A 2006 review lists the roles expected of retinoic acid precursors as renewing epidermal cells, acting as UV filters, limiting oxidative stress, controlling skin bacteria and improving ageing and photoageing.[4] That review ranked retinaldehyde as the most effective cosmeceutical retinoid and described esters as the gentlest.[4]

Retinol-type products have been sold as over-the-counter cosmetics in the US since 1984, according to Wikipedia, and EU and UK rules under Commission Regulation 2024/996, effective November 2025, set limits of 0.05 percent retinol equivalent in body lotion and 0.3 percent in other leave-on and rinse-off products, with mandatory labelling.[7]

Retinyl palmitate is added to low-fat milk and dairy products to replace vitamin A removed with the fat, and it is used as a supplement and, in injectable form, as treatment for vitamin A deficiency.[3]

Dietary retinoids are needed for growth, vision, immune function, reproduction and skin barrier function, and the body must obtain them from food.[2] Retinol is esterified by lecithin-retinol acyltransferase (LRAT) for storage, a step shown to be essential for retinyl ester accumulation in liver and eye,[8] and released by retinyl ester hydrolases; hormone-sensitive lipase can also hydrolyse retinyl esters.[1][3][9] Retinyl esters are substrates in the visual cycle, where RPE65 converts them toward 11-cis-retinal.[10][3]

In the liver, stellate cells hold most of the body's retinyl ester stores, which are mobilised as retinol when needed.[11] In cosmetic use the esters sit at the start of a multi-step route to retinoic acid, so each conversion step reduces the amount that reaches receptors; this is the reason reviews describe them as mild.[4][3]

Wikipedia's hypervitaminosis A article states that the liver stores 80 to 90 percent of preformed vitamin A, mostly in hepatic stellate cells, and that fasting retinyl ester levels above 10 percent of total circulating vitamin A are used as a marker of chronic toxicity, because serum retinol stays stable across widely different intakes.[12] Retinyl palmitate is the form animals store most of their vitamin A in, and the stabilising palmitate ester is why it is used to fortify low-fat milk.[3]

Wikipedia's retinoid article groups retinoids into four generations by structure and receptor selectivity: first-generation natural retinoic acids such as tretinoin and isotretinoin, second-generation oral-only etretinate and acitretin, third-generation aromatic compounds such as adapalene, bexarotene and tazarotene, and fourth-generation trifarotene, approved in the US in 2019.[6] The cosmetic literature uses a different ladder of retinoic acid, retinaldehyde, retinol and retinyl esters ordered by potency and irritation, with esters at the mild end.[4][5]

Retinol and retinal are described as precursors converted into retinoic acids in target tissues when needed; all-trans and 9-cis retinoic acid bind retinoic acid receptors (RARs) and retinoid X receptors (RXRs).[6] The same article states that retinyl esters are not significant RAR or RXR agonists themselves, are routine parts of the diet, and that it reports no evidence of harm from topical use.[6]

Tretinoin, the prescription reference, is all-trans retinoic acid. Wikipedia records that it was developed for acne by James Fulton and Albert Kligman at the University of Pennsylvania in the 1960s and approved by the FDA for acne in 1971; its article notes that the body makes retinoic acid from retinol, retinyl esters or beta-carotene, and that tretinoin skips those conversion steps.[13] Topical tretinoin is described as the most extensively studied retinoid for photoaging.[13]

Reviews summarising the cosmetic retinoid literature disagree in emphasis. The 2025 review reports that retinol, retinyl esters and retinaldehyde in cosmeceuticals are efficacious, safe and well tolerated.[5] The 2006 review characterised retinol and retinyl esters as non-irritant with a modest clinical effect.[4] A BMJ Clinical Evidence review of wrinkle treatments covered prescription tretinoin and other interventions among the options for photodamage.[14]

Studies of the parent compound give a sense of what topical retinol-type products do. Wikipedia's retinol article states that clinical studies have examined retinol's effect on fine wrinkles and roughness of the face and neck, that improvement is seen but is not maintained after use stops, and that very little is absorbed systemically through skin.[7] It notes that the article does not compare esters with retinol directly.[7]

No trials of retinyl esters applied to skin as a stand-alone ingredient for appearance exist; the cosmetic evidence is in narrative reviews that group esters with other first-generation retinoids.[4][5] Related human work covers vitamin A status and absorption, for example a completed 2024 trial (n=58) of vitamin A absorption from fortified bouillon.[15]

Preformed vitamin A in excess can cause hypervitaminosis A, and intake is advised to stay within recommended allowances; the World Health Organization advises limits on preformed vitamin A during pregnancy.[3]

Retinyl palmitate in sunscreens drew public attention in 2010 after animal studies in which topical retinyl palmitate or retinoic acid increased tumour rates in UV-exposed mice, and a US senator raised the issue. A 2010 toxicological analysis reported no convincing evidence that retinyl palmitate is carcinogenic in sunscreens, while a 2012 National Toxicology Program report on SKH-1 mice found that adding retinoic acid or retinyl palmitate to a cream base worsened tumour rates.[3]

Wikipedia's retinol article notes a common side effect of topical retinoids is 'retinoid dermatitis' with redness, scaling, dryness and itching, and that excess preformed vitamin A in early pregnancy is associated with birth defects; the FDA is cited as advising pregnant women to get vitamin A from beta-carotene foods and to take no more than 5,000 IU of preformed vitamin A per day, if any.[7] The WHO recommendation cited on the retinyl palmitate page says up to 10,000 IU a day during pregnancy is expected to benefit mother and fetus with little risk of harm.[3] These figures apply to dietary vitamin A, not specifically to cosmetic use; the retinoid article says oral retinoids are prohibited in people who may become pregnant unless pregnancy is prevented and that topical tretinoin is not recommended in the first trimester out of caution.[6]

Hypervitaminosis A is described as toxicity from excess preformed vitamin A, including retinyl esters. Early symptoms include headache, nausea, dizziness and irritability; signs include dry lips and eyes, hair loss, skin peeling, bone pain and raised intracranial pressure, and reported adult upper intake levels are 3,000 micrograms per day.[12] The retinoid article adds that trials found sub-toxic vitamin A supplementation increased mortality and cancer rates in smokers and asbestos workers.[6] Historical cases include Gerrit de Veer's crew falling ill after eating polar bear liver in 1597.[12]

Retinyl palmitate appears on ingredient lists of moisturisers, eye creams, lip products and sunscreens, usually as a gentler alternative to retinol, and its presence on labels is the subject of ingredient-watching content online.[3] Users who find stronger retinoids drying or irritating describe ester products as an easier starting point, according to the cosmetic reviews' emphasis on tolerance.[4][5]

Ingredient lists are the community-facing side of the topic: retinyl palmitate appears in moisturisers, eye creams, lip products and sunscreens, and some consumers look for it on labels, while others avoid it because of the sunscreen discussion.[3] On T Nation, a 2010 discussion of vitamin A deficiency and catabolism and a 2017 post on overlooked foods referenced vitamin A and retinyl esters in the diet context, which is the main way the compounds appear in lifter forums.[16][17]

timeline.event: Gerrit de Veer's crew becomes ill after eating polar bear liver, an early recorded case of vitamin A toxicity.[12]
FDA approves tretinoin for acne, the prescription retinoic acid that cosmetic retinoids are compared with.[13]
Retinol begins to be used in over-the-counter cosmetics in the US.[7]
Rpe65 shown to be required for 11-cis-retinal production from retinyl esters in the visual cycle.[10]
LRAT shown to be essential for accumulation of retinyl esters in eye and liver.[8]
Review 'Retinoids in cosmeceuticals' places retinyl esters as the mildest cosmetic retinoids.[4]
Sunscreen retinyl palmitate debate; a toxicological analysis finds no convincing evidence of carcinogenicity.[3]
National Toxicology Program report on SKH-1 mice finds worsened tumour rates with added retinyl palmitate.[3]
Fourth-generation retinoid trifarotene approved in the US.[6]
